issues.legal_issue: An unregistered lease instrument may be used to establish the fact that a tenancy was created, even though it cannot create a lease for a term requiring registration.
material_facts: The parties entered into an unregistered agreement for occupation of the premises and acted on the tenancy by the tenants occupying the premises and paying rent.
The dispute required determination of whether a tenancy existed and what kind of tenancy arose.
issues.conclusion: The unregistered agreement could be admitted and relied upon to prove the factum of the tenancy, but it did not create a lease exceeding one year; the tenancy arising from the parties’ conduct was a month-to-month tenancy.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 17(1)(d) and 49 of the Registration Act, 1908, and Section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, an instrument requiring registration cannot create the relevant lease if unregistered. However, the court may determine from other evidence and the parties’ conduct whether a tenancy arose, and an unregistered instrument may be relied on to prove that fact. The Court applied Anthony v. K.C. Ittoop & Sons, which held that a lease may arise by conduct despite an unregistered instrument, while the instrument cannot create a lease exceeding one year.

predicates.tenancy_evidence_dispute: The parties disputed whether a tenancy existed or what tenancy arose from their dealings.
predicates.unregistered_lease_instrument: The parties made an instrument concerning occupation of immovable property, but it was not registered.
predicates.parties_acted_as_landlord_and_tenant: One party occupied the premises and the other accepted rent or otherwise acted as landlord.

issues.definition: When a tenancy dispute concerns an unregistered instrument and the parties acted as landlord and tenant, the instrument may be used to establish that a tenancy existed.

issues.legal_issue: A termination restriction in an unregistered lease cannot displace the statutory rule allowing termination of a month-to-month tenancy by valid notice.
material_facts: The parties’ unregistered agreement provided that the landlord could terminate the tenancy only following specified breaches and the tenants’ failure to remedy them after notice.
The tenants occupied the premises under a month-to-month tenancy arising from the unregistered agreement.
The landlord served a notice terminating the tenancy, and the notice’s validity was not challenged.
issues.conclusion: The restriction on termination in the unregistered agreement could not override the statutory termination rule; the tenancy could be terminated by the valid notice.
issues.legal_principle: Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, supplies the rule for termination of a tenancy in the absence of a valid contract to the contrary. Read with Sections 106 and 107, an unregistered instrument cannot establish a valid contractual term that derogates from that statutory rule. The Court relied on Ram Kumar Das v. Jagadish Chandra Deb Dhabal, Samir Mukherjee v. Davinder K. Bajaj, and K.B. Saha & Sons Pvt. Ltd. v. Development Consultant Ltd. for the requirement that a contract to the contrary must be valid and that an important term of an unregistered instrument cannot be used to alter the parties’ legal rights.

rule.if: landlord_recovery_proceeding and month_to_month_tenancy and unregistered_lease_restricts_termination and landlord_served_valid_termination_notice

predicates.landlord_recovery_proceeding: A landlord brought a proceeding to recover possession after seeking to end a tenancy.
predicates.month_to_month_tenancy: The tenant occupied the premises under a tenancy that operated from month to month.
predicates.unregistered_lease_restricts_termination: An unregistered instrument stated that the landlord could terminate only in specified circumstances or after specified steps.
predicates.landlord_served_valid_termination_notice: The landlord served a notice that met the applicable requirements for terminating the tenancy.

issues.definition: In a landlord’s possession proceeding, a valid termination notice ends a month-to-month tenancy despite a termination restriction contained in an unregistered lease instrument.

issues.legal_issue: A suit need not be remanded to reconsider the validity of a termination notice merely because an unregistered lease instrument was admitted as an exhibit.
material_facts: The trial court decreed recovery of possession after treating the tenancy as month-to-month and the termination notice as valid.
The High Court set aside the decree and remanded the suit for reconsideration of the notice, directing the trial court to consider the admitted unregistered agreement.
The validity of the termination notice itself was not challenged.
issues.conclusion: The remand was unwarranted; the High Court’s order was set aside and the trial court’s decree was restored.
issues.legal_principle: An unregistered instrument may be considered to establish the factum of a tenancy, but its terms cannot be used to derogate from Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. Because the notice’s validity was not in dispute and the instrument’s termination clause could not alter the statutory rule, reconsideration on remand was unnecessary. The Court applied Anthony v. K.C. Ittoop & Sons and the principles concerning unregistered instruments stated in K.B. Saha & Sons Pvt. Ltd. v. Development Consultant Ltd.

rule.if: appeal_from_remand_order and trial_court_decreed_possession and high_court_remanded_for_notice_reconsideration and notice_validity_undisputed and remand_relied_on_unregistered_lease_terms

predicates.appeal_from_remand_order: A party appealed an order that had sent a case back to the trial court for further consideration.
predicates.trial_court_decreed_possession: The trial court had ordered the tenant to give up possession of the premises.
predicates.high_court_remanded_for_notice_reconside: The appellate court sent the case back for the trial court to reconsider the termination notice.
predicates.notice_validity_undisputed: Neither party challenged whether the termination notice was valid.
predicates.remand_relied_on_unregistered_lease_term: The reason for remanding included reconsideration of terms contained in an unregistered lease instrument.

issues.definition: When an appellate remand requires reconsideration of an undisputed termination notice by reference to an unregistered lease’s terms, the remand is unwarranted and the trial court’s possession decree is restored.
